section_summary: This section covers diplomatic communications and military intelligence reports from mid-July to late October 1945 concerning the custody, seizure, and exploitation of Japanese diplomatic and consular archives, property, and technical secrets following Japan's surrender. Early documents trace State Department and Allied coordination across neutral and belligerent countries—including Mozambique, Peru, Guatemala, Panama, Cuba, Portugal, Brazil, and Colombia—to secure Japanese official records and embassy facilities from protecting powers and prevent destruction. The remainder of the section consists of extensive intelligence reports compiled by G-2 USFET and the U.S. Strategic Bombing Survey based on captured German archives, Berlin embassy records, and interrogations of German industrialists and diplomats detailing wartime technical cooperation in synthetic fuels, nitrogen, armaments, aircraft, naval equipment, and chemical production.

subfiles.about: Inquires about Japanese letters found in German consular archives in Lourenço Marques and requests their transfer to the British Embassy after State Department examination.
subfiles.from: F. C. Everson, British Embassy, Washington
subfiles.summary: F. C. Everson of the British Embassy in Washington writes to Erle R. Dickover regarding Japanese-language correspondence discovered among German consular archives in Lourenço Marques. Respective Consuls General agreed that the letters would be forwarded to Washington for review. Everson requests that the original documents be turned over to the British Embassy once the State Department has examined them.
subfiles.title: Letter from F. C. Everson to Erle R. Dickover Regarding Japanese Letters in Lourenço Marques
subfiles.to: Erle R. Dickover, Department of State

subfiles.about: Records the filing of a memorandum concerning Japanese letters found among German consular archives in Lourenço Marques.
subfiles.from: Foreign Activity Correlation (FC)
subfiles.summary: A State Department cross-reference sheet referencing a memorandum dated November 2, 1945, from Foreign Activity Correlation. It concerns Japanese-language correspondence taken from German consular archives in Lourenço Marques and forwarded under file number F.W. 894.414/7-1645.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Foreign Activity Correlation Memorandum Regarding Japanese Letters

subfiles.about: Recommends transferring original Japanese letters from Lourenço Marques to the British Embassy while retaining summary copies and the right of recall.
subfiles.from: P. F. Cherp, Foreign Activity Correlation (FC)
subfiles.summary: P. F. Cherp of Foreign Activity Correlation responds to William T. Turner regarding Japanese letters received from Lourenço Marques with despatch No. 556. Given the unimportant nature of their contents, FC does not object to giving the originals and summaries to the British in compliance with their request. However, it suggests providing them without a statement on further disposition so that the U.S. retains the right to ask for their return if necessary.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from P. F. Cherp to William T. Turner on Disposition of Japanese Letters
subfiles.to: William T. Turner, Division of Japanese Affairs (JA)

subfiles.about: Submits an extract translation report on Japanese letters from Lourenço Marques and requests advice on their final disposition.
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, Division of Japanese Affairs (JA)
subfiles.summary: William T. Turner transmits three copies of a summary report covering Japanese letters from Lourenço Marques received via Oscar S. Strauss. Examination revealed that the longest letters were written by women concerning family matters, so extracts focused on individual movements within Japan's Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere were prepared. Turner requests advice on whether to ask the British Embassy to return the originals after inspection or allow them to dispose of them as they see fit.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from William T. Turner to R. E. Carroll Transmitting Summary of Japanese Letters
subfiles.to: R. E. Carroll, Foreign Activity Correlation (FC)

subfiles.about: Transmits original Japanese letters found in Lourenço Marques and a State Department summary report to the British Embassy.
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, Chief, Division of Japanese Affairs
subfiles.summary: William T. Turner replies to F. C. Everson's letter of July 16, 1945, enclosing the Japanese-language letters recovered from the former German Consulate General in Lourenço Marques along with a summary prepared by the Department. Turner notes that since most letters date from August 1942, their informational value is limited, though they may aid in identifying personnel involved in Japan's Greater East Asia program.
subfiles.title: Letter from William T. Turner to F. C. Everson Transmitting Japanese Letters and Summary
subfiles.to: F. C. Everson, British Embassy, Washington

subfiles.about: Urges immediate Four-Power approaches to Sweden to secure Japanese archives held by the Swedish Legation in Lima before they are destroyed.
subfiles.from: William D. Pawley, U.S. Ambassador to Peru
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Pawley reports that following consultations with British and Chinese representatives, securing Japanese archives in Peru requires delicate handling to obtain them intact. There is concern that Japanese employees of the Swedish Legation might attempt to destroy them, and the Peruvian Foreign Minister has a pro-Axis brother. Pawley recommends that the Four Powers ask the Swedish Government to instruct its Lima Legation to turn over the archives directly to Allied representatives, avoiding delays previously experienced with German records.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 853 from Lima Regarding Securing Japanese Archives in Peru

subfiles.about: Reports that no Japanese diplomatic archives exist in Guatemala due to the lack of Japanese diplomatic representation.
subfiles.from: Edwin Jackson Kyle, U.S. Ambassador to Guatemala
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Kyle responds to the State Department circular telegram of August 14 regarding enemy records. He confirms that there are no Japanese archives in Guatemala because Japan maintained no diplomatic representation in the country.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 511 from Guatemala City Confirming Absence of Japanese Archives

subfiles.about: Details the Panamanian Foreign Office's unofficial seizure of Japanese Legation archives, safes, and property, and arrangements for Allied access and storage.
subfiles.from: Walter J. Donnelly, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires in Panama
subfiles.summary: Donnelly reports on a conference with the President and Foreign Minister of Panama alongside British and Chinese Ministers, resulting in the Panamanian Foreign Office taking unofficial possession of Japanese Legation archives, three safes, and property. The Swiss honorary consul has requested authority from Caracas to make an official transfer, after which all archives will be made available to the U.S. Embassy. Furniture and office equipment will be stored in an Army warehouse in the Canal Zone with General Brett's cooperation, and two Packard cars were requested on loan by Panama.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 766 from Panama Regarding Takeover of Japanese Archives and Property

subfiles.about: Reports joint Allied approaches to the Cuban Minister of State and Spanish Chargé d'Affaires to obtain Japanese archives and property in Cuba.
subfiles.from: R. Henry Norweb, U.S. Ambassador to Cuba
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Norweb describes joint diplomatic representations made by the U.S., British, Chinese, and Soviet missions requesting custody of Japanese archives and property from the Cuban Government and the Spanish Chargé d'Affaires. The Cuban Ministry of State noted the legal distinction from Germany, since a Japanese government still exists under Allied control, and asked how Washington is handling protecting powers. The Spanish Chargé confirmed that the archives are wired and sealed in boxes and is requesting authority from Madrid to transfer them to Cuba on behalf of the Allies.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 540 from Habana on Allied Request for Japanese Archives in Cuba

subfiles.about: Reports the Portuguese Foreign Office's refusal to surrender Japanese archives without authorization from the legitimate Japanese Government.
subfiles.from: Herman B. Baruch, U.S. Ambassador to Portugal
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Baruch reports that British and Chinese missions in Lisbon have not yet received instructions regarding Japanese archives. The Portuguese Foreign Office stated that although willing to cooperate, it finds no legal justification for turning over Japanese property or archives to Allied powers. Portugal highlighted that unlike Germany, where the legitimate government collapsed, the Japanese Government and its diplomatic mission in Lisbon still legally exist; Portugal hopes the Allies can instruct Tokyo to authorize the transfer upon formal surrender.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1741 from Lisbon on Portuguese Stance Regarding Japanese Archives

subfiles.about: Recommends centralized State Department custody, physical transfer procedures, and inter-agency access rules for Japanese diplomatic and consular archives in the U.S.
subfiles.from: R. E. Hibbard, Special War Problems Division (SWP)
subfiles.summary: SWP outlines recommendations for taking custody of Japanese diplomatic and consular property and archives from protecting powers (Switzerland for the continental U.S., Sweden for Hawaii). It proposes placing sole responsibility with the State Department, having the Chief Special Agent take physical custody, centralizing all archives in Washington at the Japanese Embassy building with photostat facilities, and making them accessible to interested U.S. agencies and reciprocal Allies. The memorandum also details staffing, security against dissipation, and initial emergency financing.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from R. E. Hibbard to General Holmes on Custody Policy for Japanese Archives in the U.S.
subfiles.to: Julius C. Holmes, Assistant Secretary of State (A-H)

subfiles.about: Records the temporary charge-out and retrieval of file materials from decimal file 894.414.
subfiles.from: Department of State Records Service Center
subfiles.summary: Standard Department of State Form DS-1033 recording the charging out of file items under decimal classification 894.414 on November 4, 1960. It specifies charge details and administrative routing within the archives.
subfiles.title: Charge-Out Record Form DS-1033 for Decimal File 894.414

subfiles.about: Reports that a preliminary search of former Japanese Legation archives in Panama revealed no valuable intelligence as records and codes were destroyed.
subfiles.from: Walter J. Donnelly, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires in Panama
subfiles.summary: Donnelly reports that an initial examination of the former Japanese Legation archives seized in Panama revealed no information of value, indicating that correspondence and code books had been destroyed prior to seizure. U.S. Embassy staff and local intelligence agencies on the Isthmus are investigating additional potential leads and will inform the Department if any useful material is discovered.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 771 from Panama on Results of Japanese Legation Archives Search

subfiles.about: Reports Brazilian arrangements with the Swedish Legation to take custody of Japanese archives and grant full access to the U.S. Embassy.
subfiles.from: Adolf A. Berle, Jr., U.S. Ambassador to Brazil
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Berle reports that Brazilian Foreign Office Secretary General Muniz expects the Swedish Legation to surrender Japanese archives early the following week. Muniz requested the Swedish Minister remove the Japanese caretaker custodian and ordered Brazilian police to guard the premises to prevent document destruction. The Swedish Minister agreed to notify the Embassy upon receiving instructions, and Muniz confirmed the U.S. Embassy will receive complete access to the records once received.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 2588 from Rio de Janeiro on Securing Japanese Archives in Brazil

subfiles.about: Argues on legal and diplomatic grounds against seizing Japanese archives and property outright, urging adherence to the Potsdam Declaration and protecting power custody.
subfiles.from: Joseph W. Ballantine, Director, Office of Far Eastern Affairs (FE)
subfiles.summary: Ballantine comments on SWP's August 17 memorandum to General Holmes regarding Japanese property and archives in the U.S. While agreeing that intelligence should be exploited to implement the Potsdam Declaration, FE stresses that unlike Germany, the Japanese Government continues to exist under the surrender terms. Ballantine argues that the U.S. should direct Tokyo to authorize examination and copying by Allied personnel on the premises under protecting power custody, rather than unilaterally confiscating or disposing of property, thereby upholding American honor and international commitments.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Joseph W. Ballantine to SWP Questioning Legal Basis for Seizing Japanese Archives
subfiles.to: Frederick A. Plitt, Special War Problems Division (SWP)

subfiles.about: Inquires whether the U.S. Embassy or Panamanian Government should take possession of Japanese vehicles and furniture, noting pending Swiss authorization.
subfiles.from: Walter J. Donnelly, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires in Panama
subfiles.summary: Donnelly reports that the Swiss Honorary Consul in Panama has not yet received authorization from the Swiss Legation in Caracas to turn over Japanese property and archives. The archives remain stored in the Panamanian Foreign Office awaiting release. Donnelly inquires when similar transactions will take place in the U.S. and asks whether the Embassy should take custody of the large quantities of furniture and motor vehicles or allow Panama to retain them.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 781 from Panama Inquiring on Japanese Property Disposition

subfiles.about: Reports that the Spanish Chargé d'Affaires is still waiting for instructions from Madrid to relinquish Japanese archives and asks if Washington can expedite the process.
subfiles.from: R. Henry Norweb, U.S. Ambassador to Cuba
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Norweb informs the State Department that the Spanish Chargé d'Affaires in Havana has not yet received instructions from the Spanish Foreign Office in Madrid authorizing the release of Japanese archives. The Chargé is personally eager to divest himself of the material. Norweb asks whether the Department can help expedite the dispatch of these instructions from Madrid.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 559 from Habana on Delay in Madrid Instructions Regarding Japanese Archives

subfiles.about: Reports Soviet opposition to unilateral U.S. custody of Japanese archives in Colombia and describes measures taken to secure sealed archives at the Japanese Legation.
subfiles.from: John C. Wiley, U.S. Ambassador to Colombia
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Wiley reports that the Soviet Minister in Bogota objected on principle to turning over Japanese archives to the American Embassy on behalf of all Allies, while the British Ambassador dismissed the objection given the lack of Japanese linguists. Meanwhile, the Swiss Chargé is indisposed, but a clerk revealed that substantial sealed archives remain at the former Japanese Legation where the Swiss Chancellor and a Japanese gardener reside. Suspecting the gardener was entrusted with confidential files, Wiley enlisted the Legal Attaché and Colombian police for discreet surveillance and requested the archives be moved to the Swiss Legation.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1133 from Bogota on Soviet Opposition and Status of Japanese Archives in Colombia

subfiles.about: Reports that the Salvadoran Foreign Office delivered Japanese archives to the U.S. Embassy and requests instructions on their final disposition.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, San Salvador
subfiles.summary: The American Embassy in San Salvador reports that the Salvadoran Foreign Office delivered the Japanese archives to the Embassy on August 27 following the Department's circular telegram of August 14. British and Chinese colleagues have been notified of the transfer. The Embassy urgently requests instructions on the final disposition of the records, noting that its storage space is already overtaxed.
subfiles.title: Airgram A-200 from San Salvador on Delivery of Japanese Archives

subfiles.about: Transmits G-2 USFET intelligence reports (J-048 to J-058) and document reports (CD-124 to CD-145) on Japanese military, industrial, and diplomatic matters.
subfiles.from: Robert Murphy, U.S. Political Adviser for Germany, Frankfurt
subfiles.summary: Robert Murphy transmits intelligence and documentary reports prepared by the Office of the Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, USFET, regarding Japanese activities and German-Japanese collaboration. The despatch lists seven Japanese Intelligence Reports (J-048 through J-058) covering gas hydrogenation, military purchases, naval offices, naval stores, shipyards, Foreign Office personnel, and oil/chemical industries, as well as twenty-two Document Reports (CD-124 through CD-145). Original underlying documents were forwarded to the Military Intelligence Research Section (MIRS) in Washington.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 892 from Robert Murphy Transmitting Japanese Intelligence and Document Reports

subfiles.about: Summarizes pre-contract correspondence between I.G. Farben, Krupp, and Japanese firms regarding synthetic fuel, natural gas, and coal hydrogenation plants.
subfiles.from: Dupré Sassard, Lt. Colonel, GSC, Executive, G-2 USFET
subfiles.summary: Report J-048 presents translated extracts from pre-contract files between I.G. Farben in Germany and its Tokyo branch, Krupp, and steel suppliers from 1937 to 1942, recovered by the U.S. Seventh Army. It details Japanese efforts to develop natural gas and coal hydrogenation using the Haber-Bosch and Uhde processes in Formosa, Manchuria (Fushun), North Korea, and Japan proper (Tokuyama, Niigata). Records include discussions between Foreign Minister Matsuoka and I.G. Farben representatives in Berlin, high-pressure reaction vessel manufacturing constraints, and coal analyses for synthetic gas production.
subfiles.title: Japanese Intelligence Report J-048: Japan, Hydrogenation of Gases in
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department, and Distribution List

subfiles.about: Reports the recovery and exploitation of vast quantities of documents and film from the Japanese Embassy in Berlin regarding Army and Navy purchases.
subfiles.from: Dupré Sassard, Lt. Colonel, GSC, Executive, G-2 USFET
subfiles.summary: Report J-053 describes the exploitation of documents and an enormous library recovered from the damaged and looted Japanese Embassy at Tiergartenstrasse in Berlin by the Japanese Intelligence Section and British G.S.I. Material recovered from rubble includes correspondence on Japanese Army and Navy material purchases in Germany. A film of the Japanese coast and two folders of purchase records were dispatched by air courier to G-2 MIRS in Washington.
subfiles.title: Japanese Intelligence Report J-053: Germany, Japanese Army and Navy Purchases of Material in
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department, and Distribution List

subfiles.about: Compiles technical data on Japanese naval shipbuilding yards, government and private dry docks, and French Indo-China ports from captured German naval handbooks.
subfiles.from: Dupré Sassard, Lt. Colonel, GSC, Executive, G-2 USFET
subfiles.summary: Report J-056 extracts data from a captured German Naval Staff handbook ('Handbuch für Admiralstabsoffiziere') and French hydrographic reports. It outlines Japanese fleet construction capacities for battleships, aircraft carriers, cruisers, destroyers, and submarines across major shipyards (Kure, Yokosuka, Sasebo, Kobe, Nagasaki, Uraga, Maizuru). Comprehensive dimensional tables detail government and commercial dry docks across Japan proper, Dairen, Port Arthur, Keelung, and Fusan, followed by navigational and drydock data for Indo-China ports including Saigon, Cam Ranh, Tourane, and Haiphong.
subfiles.title: Japanese Intelligence Report J-056: Japan/Indo-China, Shipyards, Drydocks, and Harbors
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department, and Distribution List

subfiles.about: Investigates the evacuated Japanese Naval Attaché's office in Berlin-Charlottenburg and traces the departure routes of key naval officers.
subfiles.from: Dupré Sassard, Lt. Colonel, GSC, Executive, G-2 USFET
subfiles.summary: Report J-054 documents the investigation of the evacuated Japanese naval office at Berliner Strasse 93 in Charlottenburg, Berlin. The housekeeper reported that naval officers including Admiral Kojima, Admiral Abe, Captain Taniguchi, Captain Miura, and Captain Ikeda occupied the premises until late March 1945, departing for Constance, the Baltic to reach Sweden, or U-boat embarkation points. An inquiry at a German Admiralty facility on Uhland Strasse revealed that Soviet naval forces had already evacuated most records, leaving nothing relating to the Far East.
subfiles.title: Japanese Intelligence Report J-054: Japanese Naval Attaché's Office, Berlin
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department, and Distribution List

subfiles.about: Details the discovery and seizure of 200 packing cases of German and Italian naval stores and aircraft equipment in Kiel intended for shipment to Japan.
subfiles.from: Dupré Sassard, Lt. Colonel, GSC, Executive, G-2 USFET
subfiles.summary: Report J-055 quotes U.S. and Royal Navy reports regarding 200 cases of naval stores seized at Hamburger Chaussee in Kiel, reported by anti-Nazi property owner Bernard Elsbrock. The goods were arranged by retired Korvettenkapitän Becker, who had warned Elsbrock not to reveal them to the Allies. Sample inspections revealed bombsights, radar and radio gear, aircraft film equipment, pressure flasks, and Italian aircraft gun specifications from Ansaldo, with original labels pasted over with Japanese shipping instructions; additional unexamined consignments were noted at Schönberg, Friedrichsort, and Elmshorn.
subfiles.title: Japanese Intelligence Report J-055: Germany, Shipment of Naval Stores to Japan
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department, and Distribution List

subfiles.about: Interrogates German Foreign Office officials Georg Martius and Wilhelm Tannenberg concerning German-Japanese economic relations, trade negotiations, and evacuated records.
subfiles.from: Dupré Sassard, Lt. Colonel, GSC, Executive, G-2 USFET
subfiles.summary: Report J-057 records interrogations conducted by Hartley Ayers and Lt. Walter Jessel of SHAEF G-2 Economic Section at Augsburg with German diplomats Georg Martius and Wilhelm Tannenberg. Tannenberg, former Vice Consul in Chicago, described the negotiation of the 1943 General Commercial Treaty as largely political window dressing, recalled that Pearl Harbor caught the German Embassy completely by surprise, and provided details on key personnel handling Far Eastern affairs. He also mapped the evacuation of Commercial Department and Far Eastern archives from Berlin to Silesia and Thuringia, and noted Japanese procurement priorities in special steels, aluminum, and machine tools.
subfiles.title: Japanese Intelligence Report J-057: Germany, Foreign Office Personnel, Information re Japanese
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department, and Distribution List

subfiles.about: Transmits preliminary U.S. Strategic Bombing Survey investigations and German industrial interrogations analyzing Japanese synthetic oil, nitrogen, and chemical production.
subfiles.from: Dupré Sassard, Lt. Colonel, GSC, Executive, G-2 USFET
subfiles.summary: Report J-058 transmits a preliminary investigation by the Oil Division of the U.S. Strategic Bombing Survey based on captured documents and interrogations of over 25 German chemical and industrial experts. The report assesses aviation gasoline, synthetic nitrogen, methanol, and nitric acid as Japan's most critical bottlenecks, evaluating industrial capacities, target vulnerabilities, and clandestine German-Japanese technology transfers including ethylene dibromide shipments. Transcripts of detailed interrogations with engineering representatives of Friedrich Uhde K.G. and Dr. C. Otto & Co. describe the design, construction, and operational challenges of synthetic ammonia, coke oven, coal hydrogenation, and tar distillation plants across Japan, Korea, and Manchuria.
subfiles.title: Japanese Intelligence Report J-058: Japan, Oil, Chemical and Rubber Industries
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department, and Distribution List
